title: Agricultural productivity can expand food supply and farm income while fertilizer shocks, unequal capacity, diet change, and emissions keep food security exposed
source_unit: OECD and Food and Agriculture Organization, OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook 2026-2035
geography: Global, regional, and national agricultural commodities and aquatic-food markets with low-, middle-, and high-income comparisons

denominator.unit: global agricultural commodity and aquatic-food market projection frame

production_growth.unit: percent projected expansion in global agricultural production over the next decade

income_per_worker.unit: percent projected increase in global gross agricultural income per worker by 2035

growth_driver.value: productivity improvements and intensification drive most projected production growth

uncertainty.value: natural and economic variability leaves a 25 percent chance of a decline in workers' income relative to the projected baseline

observations.method: OECD-FAO Aglink-Cosimo model and comparative agricultural-market analysis using data through 2025.
observations.uncertainty: These are baseline projections and risk scenarios, not realized outcomes; weather, policy, conflict, prices, technology, and trade can shift the path.
observations.subgroup: Farm workers, smallholders, agricultural firms, consumers, food-importing countries, low-income economies, and rural communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Productivity growth can improve food availability and rural income while diversification, insurance, and trade reduce exposure to shocks.

observations.period: 2026; Middle East conflict, fertilizer use, and cereal production

denominator.unit: global agricultural-input, cereal-production, food-price, and geopolitical-shock frame

shock_channel.value: economic disruptions associated with the 2026 Middle East conflict are expected to constrain fertilizer use

cereal_effect.value: reduced fertilizer use is expected to decrease cereal production, especially in low-income countries

household_effect.value: income losses and higher food prices could force lower-income households to reduce food consumption or shift toward cheaper foods

resilience_difference.value: higher-income households are generally expected to maintain dietary patterns more readily than lower-income households

observations.method: OECD-FAO model scenario assessing slower growth and higher energy and fertilizer costs associated with the 2026 geopolitical shock.
observations.uncertainty: The scenario is not a household food diary or realized price forecast; the distribution of effects depends on policy, exchange rates, trade, stocks, and local production.
observations.subgroup: Low-income households, food-importing countries, cereal producers, children, rural workers, food retailers, and consumers with limited dietary room.
observations.counterinterpretation: Substitution, public support, food reserves, local production, and trade rerouting can buffer a fertilizer or cereal shock, though not evenly.

denominator.unit: global agricultural production, direct greenhouse-gas emissions, and sustainability frame

direct_emissions.unit: percent projected increase in direct agricultural greenhouse-gas emissions over the outlook period

livestock_share.unit: percent of the projected emissions increase attributed to growing animal herds

fertilizer_share.unit: percent of the projected emissions increase attributed to higher nitrous-oxide emissions from synthetic fertilizers

productivity_challenge.value: the policy challenge is to accelerate sustainable productivity so emissions grow more slowly or decline relative to current values

observations.method: OECD-FAO baseline projection of agricultural production, livestock, fertilizer use, and direct agricultural emissions.
observations.uncertainty: The projections exclude some indirect lifecycle effects and depend on technology, land use, diets, policy, and model assumptions; they do not establish local environmental outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Farmers, livestock producers, fertilizer users, consumers, climate-exposed communities, policymakers, and food-system workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technology, breeding, feed, land management, reduced loss, dietary shifts, and better input efficiency could reduce emissions intensity even as total demand grows.

observations.period: 2026-2035; dietary transition, rural poverty, and trade

denominator.unit: global and regional food consumption, agricultural labor productivity, trade, and nutrition frame

southeast_asia_consumption.unit: percent estimated share of global consumption growth from Southeast Asia by 2035

diet_diversification.value: urbanization and income gains are expected to shift diets toward greater shares of livestock and fish products in many lower-middle-income countries

low_income_worker_income.value: agricultural workers in low-income regions of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia earn about USD 930 per year on average and are projected to reach around USD 1,100

trade_channel.value: international agricultural trade, infrastructure, storage, and technology remain critical to balancing supply and demand and sustaining affordable healthy diets

observations.method: OECD-FAO regional and national agricultural-market projections, labor-productivity comparisons, and food-system analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Regional averages conceal within-country inequality, informal work, nutrition quality, and differences in farm and consumer access to markets.
observations.subgroup: Low-income agricultural workers, smallholders, urban consumers, food-importing households, fishers, retailers, and communities with weak storage or transport infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trade and dietary diversification can improve access, income, and choice, while local food systems and social protection can reduce dependence on volatile global markets.

related_sources.claim: FAO Crop Prospects and Food Situation provides complementary near-term cereal and acute food-security monitoring.
FAO Food Outlook and State of Agricultural Commodity Markets provide complementary food-market and trade context.

boundary: This record adds a global agricultural-production, fertilizer-shock, farm-income, diet, emissions, trade, and food-security route. It uses OECD-FAO model projections and aggregate market analysis, not household food diaries, individual farm histories, causal price estimates, or proof that production growth delivers affordable healthy diets.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD-FAO Agricultural Outlook 2026-2035 materials were reviewed for production and income projections, Middle East fertilizer and cereal scenario, emissions, dietary transition, low-income farm-worker income, and trade/infrastructure conditions.
